title: Worlds beyond worlds
hook: there are worlds beneath worlds and skies above skies, beyond counting (Japji 22)
tomorrow: how do you make a coin out of a life?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hour of creation: not in any book, not with any scholar. Only the creator knows.

Phone lights held up at a concert, thousands of them in the dark, and for a second the crowd looks like a sky. The janamsakhis tell of an evening at the temple of Jagannath in Puri, at the hour of aarti, when lamps are waved on a platter. Guru Nanak, they say, looked up and sang of the aarti already happening overhead: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls, the scented breeze the incense, and all the forests flowers.
screen: `A CROWD OF LIGHTS.` → `EVENING AARTI AT PURI.` → `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.`

segments.voice: That's the size of sky Guru Nanak sang in, and the Japji's twenty-second stanza pushes it further. Underworlds below underworlds, it says, and a hundred thousand skies above skies. Searchers went to the very edges and grew weary, and the Vedas say so. Other scriptures speak of eighteen thousand worlds, and of one essence behind them. If it could be counted, it would be written down; but the counting runs out first. Nanak says: call Him great; He alone knows Himself. So, in the Japji, creation is beyond counting, and so is the Creator, and the fitting answer to that size is praise, not a number. A neighbor tradition looks up at the same sky. Psalm 147 says of God: "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names." Both look up, and both end in praise. They part on one point. The psalm pictures every star numbered and named by God. The Japji says any count, ours or the books', gives out, and only He knows Himself. One holds the count in God's hands; the other says no written count can hold it. And so, in the story, Guru Nanak's aarti has the whole sky for its lamps.
screen: `SKIES ABOVE SKIES.` · `THE COUNTING RUNS OUT.` · `CALL HIM GREAT.` · `PSALM 147: EVERY STAR NAMED.` · then, large: `BEYOND COUNTING.`

segments.voice: If you can, step outside or go to a window, and walk a few slow steps while looking up. Find the farthest thing you can see, a star, a cloud, a plane's light, and keep your eyes on it as you walk. Let the sky be bigger than the list in your head.
Worlds beyond worlds: the Japji's twenty-second stanza, skies above skies, more than any count can hold.
Here's the line: beyond counting, so praise instead of a number. Three of five from the Japji.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Japji each morning; Guru Nanak's sky-aarti hymn, 'gagan mai thaal', is sung in the Sikh evening prayers and in kirtan.

chat.says: walked home with theo under a huge sky. he says it makes his problems small. sad or nice?
options: The Japji's sky ends in praise, not gloom: worlds beyond counting, and 'call Him great.'
Sad. The Japji says we're so small that nothing we do really matters.
Nice, but only because the Japji says each star has your name written on it.
chat.meaning: Japji 22 counts skies above skies until the counting runs out, and answers with praise: call Him great. Smallness there turns into wonder.

tie.story: Guru Nanak sang the sky as a vast aarti, and the Japji says the worlds are beyond counting: call Him great.
tie.friend: Theo's feeling small under the sky can be wonder rather than dismissal, and Zoe can tell him so.

Unity thread: Psalm 147:4 (KJV, quoted) shares the upward look and praise; honest difference: the psalm has God number and name every star, the Japji says any count runs out. No ranking; no 'the same' claim.
